## Reading and previewing data

Our data are usually stored as a `.csv` file and after loading a `.csv` file into RStudio, we will have a "data frame". A data frame can be considered a special case of matrix where each column represents a measurement or variable of interest for each observation which correspond to the rows of the dataset. After loading the `tidyverse` suite of packages, we use the [`read_csv()`](https://readr.tidyverse.org/reference/read_delim.html) function to load the 2025 NBA regular season stats dataset from yesterday:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──

## Data manipulation with `dplyr`

An easier way to manipulate the data frame is through the `dplyr` package, which is in the `tidyverse` suite of packages. The operations we can do include: selecting specific columns, filtering for rows, re-ordering rows, adding new columns and summarizing data. The "split-apply-combine" concept can be achieved by `dplyr`.

### Selecting columns with `select()`

The function `select()` can be use to select certain column with the column names. First create a new table called `nba_stats_pg` that only contains the `player` and `games` columns:


::: {.cell}

```
:::


To select all columns except a specific column, use the `-` (subtraction) operator. For example, view the output from uncommenting the following line of code:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# select(nba_stats, -player)
```
:::


To select a range of columns by name (that are in consecutive order), use the `:` (colon) operator. For example, view the output from uncommenting the following line of code:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# select(nba_stats, player:games)
```
:::


To select all columns that start with certain character strings, use the function `starts_with()`. Other matching options are:

1.  `ends_with()`: select columns that end with a character string

2.  `contains()`: select columns that contain a character string

3.  `matches()`: select columns that match a regular expression

4.  `one_of()`: select columns names that are from a group of names


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

# select(nba_stats, starts_with("three"))
# select(nba_stats, contains("throw"))
```
:::

## Challenge exercises 

Finished early? We encourage you to review how to join dataframes in R by reading sections [19.3-19.5 of R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html#sec-mutating-joins) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. Then, try the following exercises. We challenge you to not use AI---ask the TAs if you get stuck!

### Bonus exercise 1 (Paralympic Swimming)

Load the following dataset ([link to the codebook](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2021/2021-08-03/readme.md)). Create a dataframe with the number of athletes that have medaled in swimming since 2000 for each county. Create a second dataframe with the total number of medals that each country has won in swimming since 2000. Then, join the two dataframes. Arrange the joined dataframe from greatest number of medals to least number of medals. 

Check your work: Is the number of medals always greater than or equal to the number of athletes? 

::: {.cell}

athletes <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-08-03/athletes.csv')

### Bonus exercise 2 (Ultra running)

Load the following datasets that explore trends in ultra running ([link to the data dictionary](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2021/2021-10-26/readme.md)). Your task is to identify female runners who ran at least 10 ultra races between age 30-50. Create a dataset of their race results from this time in their life. The dataset should have additional columns: 

- the distance of the race (in miles)
- the age of the runner at the time of the race (assume `age` represents the runner's age in 2021) 
- the average minutes per mile that runner completed the race in

*There is a lot going on in this one, so don't feel discouraged if you get stuck!*
